comments.text: The KERNAL's code for the key held down now ($40 for none), kept up to date by the KERNAL's own interrupt, which this program leaves running. The key reader ($18BD) compares it with the five codes at $195E.

The pointer the track reader builds from a voice's track address ($144C/$144F). $FB-$FE are the four zero-page bytes the KERNAL leaves free, and they are the only memory below $1000 the program uses: everything else down there is the machine's.
The high byte of the track pointer.
The pointer to the pattern a voice is playing, built from $2FC0/$3040 whenever it reads a note.
The high byte of the pattern pointer.
The KERNAL's lock on the character-set switch. The program sets bit 7 at the start, so that pressing Commodore and Shift cannot turn the screen's lower case into graphics.
The KERNAL's interrupt vector, $1831 in the loaded image: the raster interrupt reaches the music through the KERNAL's own handler, which saves the registers and scans the keyboard first.

Starts tune A (0-15): copies its eight-byte header from $30C0 + 8A to $144C (the low and high bytes of each voice's track, then the two tempo bytes), silences the three voices, reads each voice's first track entry ($13F9), sets the volume to 15 with the low-pass selected ($D418 = $1F) and turns the music on ($104C = $FF). Called by the key reader with the tune for the key pressed, and by nothing else: the program has no start-up tune.
$FF while the music plays, 0 when it has stopped or been silenced.

Plays the music once a frame from the raster interrupt, when it is on. For each voice, 2 down to 0 ($1454 its register offset): on a beat ($141A = 0) counts the note down ($1469) and at its end reads the next one from the voice's pattern (number $1460, address from $2FC0/$3040, place $145D); on the note's last beat it drops the gate unless the note's byte ties it to the next. Off a beat it runs the instrument's effects ($118F). Then the attack ($135C), the voice's three registers ($13AE) and the tempo counts ($13DF). Unlike Armalyte's driver this one cannot fade and has no track loops: the fade lives in the program ($1914).

The instrument's effects, every frame but the one a note starts: the pulse sweep between the instrument's two limits, vibrato after its delay, a slide from the note's extra byte, and the effect flags at +3 of the instrument: $01 alternates two waveforms frame about, $02 a two-note arpeggio, $04 drops the gate after the first beat and falls in pitch.

The attack: while the instrument's attack frames last ($14AB), effect flag $10 holds its attack waveform and $20 its attack note, and the frame the count runs out both go back to the note being played.

Writes the voice: the waveform through its gate mask to $D404, then the frequency high and low bytes. A new note that attacks has already had the gate written off and on in this frame, which restarts the envelope. Then the attack count ($14AB) and the frame count ($14AE), and on to the next voice.

The two tempo counts at the end of each frame: $141B down from $1453, and when it runs out the beat count $141A is reloaded from $1452 early, which lengthens the odd beat. With both counts 1, as all four tunes the keys play have, a beat is two frames.

Reads a voice's next track entry (track from $144C/$144F, place $145A) through the pointer $FB/$FC: a byte below $80 is a repeat count for the pattern number after it, and one of $80 up is kept as the pattern itself, where $FF starts the track again and anything else stops the music. That is the whole track language here: Armalyte's driver adds loops and a fade command.
The beat counter: notes move on when it is 0; it counts down each frame.
The second beat counter; when it runs out the first is reloaded early.
The register offset of the voice being played (0, 7 or 14).
The new instrument's attack and decay, on its way to $D405.
The new instrument's sustain and release, on its way to $D406.
The pulse sweep's step, from the instrument.
The pulse sweep's upper limit (high nibble of the instrument's limits byte).
The pulse sweep's lower limit (its low nibble).
The note byte just read, kept while the note is set up and then stored per voice at $149F.
A downward slide's step this frame.
Vibrato: the frames each way, for each of 16 kinds. Byte for byte the same table as Armalyte's ($C4BF), as are the two that follow and the frequencies.
The vibrato depth: how far the gap to the next semitone is halved, by kind.
The delays before vibrato starts, picked by the high nibble of the instrument's vibrato byte: 0, 10, 16, 25, 37, 50, 62, 75 frames.
Low bytes of the three voices' tracks for the tune playing.
High bytes of the three voices' tracks.
The tempo: frames between beats, less one.
The second tempo count: every this many frames plus one the beat restarts early.
The three voices' register offsets: 0, 7, 14.
Each voice's instrument number times 8, its place in the instrument tables.
Each voice's place in its track.
Each voice's place in its pattern.
Each voice's pattern number ($FF starts the track again, other values of $80 up stop the music).
How many more times each voice plays its pattern. A track entry of 0 means 256.
The first byte of each voice's note: the length in beats less one (bits 0-5), bit 6 for a rest, bit 7 for an extra byte.
Beats left of each voice's note.
Each voice's waveform and gate byte.
Each voice's note number (0-95).
Each voice's flag ($FF) that the instrument's attack frames are over.
Each voice's instrument number.
Each voice's gate mask: $FF, or $FE to hold the gate off.
Each voice's pulse sweep direction (0 up, 1 down).
Each voice's slide: $C0 and up slides up by the low six bits each frame, $80-$BF down.
Each voice's vibrato direction.
Frames until each voice's vibrato starts.
Each voice's vibrato depth shift, counted down to a negative to halve the step.
Each voice's vibrato phase flag.
Each voice's vibrato frame count.
Frames each way of each voice's vibrato.
Low byte of each voice's vibrato step.
High byte of each voice's vibrato step.
Low byte of each voice's frequency.
High byte of each voice's frequency.

Each voice's note byte as read. Bit 7 ties the note to the one after it: the driver reads this slot before overwriting it, so a note attacks unless the note before it on that voice was tied, and holds its gate open through its last beat when it is tied itself. Armalyte's driver puts the tie on the other end, reading the new note's own byte.
Low byte of each voice's pulse width.
High byte of each voice's pulse width.
Each voice's instrument effect flags.
Frames left of each voice's attack waveform or note.
Frames since each voice's note began; bit 0 alternates the waveform and the arpeggio.
A three-byte slot nothing reads: a tune starting clears it for each voice ($1019) and no instruction loads it. $14B4 is a second one.
The other slot nothing reads: a note starting clears it for each voice ($1186). Armalyte's driver has neither of the two, so this version of it kept a pair of variables past whatever used them.

Where the program starts, after its unpacker has put it in place and restored the ROMs ($01 = $37). It silences the SID and greys the four digits ($192B), sets $0291 so that the Commodore key cannot switch the character set under the screen's lower case, and falls into the colour bars, which are the whole of the main loop. Everything else happens in the interrupt.

The raster interrupt, reached through the KERNAL's handler at $0314: acknowledges the raster ($D019), takes the raster line before and after playing the music ($104D), leaves the difference in $18AE, draws the gauge from it ($1852), reads the keyboard ($18BD) and ends in the KERNAL's own exit ($EA7B), which restores the registers. Nothing here sets the VIC up: the raster line, the screen and the colours arrive in the loaded image, written to the chip by the last stage of the unpacker.

Draws the gauge of how long the music took: the raster lines in $18AE as a bar five cells tall, eight lines to a cell, filled from the bottom with reverse spaces and topped with one of the eight part-blocks at $18B0. The five cells are written twice each, to the screen at $0563, $058B, $05B3, $05DB and $0603, which is the two-cell column at the right of the screen, bottom cell first.
The raster lines the music took this frame, the gauge's reading.
Whole cells left to fill while the gauge is drawn.
The eight part-block characters, none to seven eighths: space, and the screen codes for a bar filled from the bottom. The remainder of the lines over eight picks one.
The gauge's five cells as screen codes, bottom first, built afresh each frame.
The gauge's second cell from the bottom, read into the screen at $05DB.
The gauge's third cell, read into the screen at $05B3.
The gauge's fourth cell, read into the screen at $058B.
The gauge's top cell, read into the screen at $0563. Five cells of eight lines each, so a full bar is 40 raster lines.

Reads the keyboard from the KERNAL's $C5: the five codes at $195E are the keys 1, 2, 3, 4 and RUN/STOP. A key is acted on once ($195D holds it until it is let go). The four digits start a tune: $1963 gives its number, and $1967 the cell in the colour map, so the digit pressed turns yellow and the others go back to grey. RUN/STOP starts the fade, and while the fade runs the keys are not read at all.
RUN/STOP: sets the fade going, unless the volume is already down, when it silences everything instead.

The fade, every frame while it runs: the volume drops by one every five frames from 15 to 0 and then everything is silenced. It is written straight to $D418, over the driver's own setting, and the driver knows nothing about it: Armalyte's version of this driver fades itself.
Silences everything: the music off, the fade off, the volume to 0, and the four digits grey. Called at the start and at the end of a fade.
Just the colours: the four digits' three cells each back to grey (15), so that the one about to be played can be turned yellow.
$FF while a key is held, so that holding 1 does not start the tune again every frame.
The five keys' codes as the KERNAL reports them in $C5: 1 ($38), 2 ($3B), 3 ($08), 4 ($0B) and RUN/STOP ($3F).
The tune each digit plays: 1 plays tune 10, 2 plays tune 3, 3 plays tune 0 and 4 plays tune 1. Four of the sixteen headers, in no particular order; the other tunes in memory have no key.
Where each digit sits in the colour map, as an offset from $D995: 0, 7, 14, 21.
$FF while the fade is running.
Frames until the fade's next step, five each time.
The volume the fade is at, 15 down to 0.

Six bytes nothing reaches: a wait for the raster to pass line 255 and a NOP, sitting just below the colour bars with four kilobytes of zeros before them. The bars wait on the raster themselves, in their own way, so this is what an earlier version of the loop did.

The main loop, which is nothing but colour bars. The top half: wait for line 15, then on each raster line to line 91, step back through the 32 colours at $2050 and write the next to the background. The index moves on by one a frame as well, so the bands crawl up the screen. Below the bars the background goes back to dark grey.
Thirty NOPs nothing reaches, between the top half of the bars and its colour table: the table is where the code that reads it expects, and the gap is padding.
Where the top bars start in their colour table this frame, 31 down to 0.
The top bars' 32 colours: black up through red and orange to white and back, then blue through green to white, then a grey-to-cyan pair of ramps, each colour twice.

The bottom half of the bars, under the text: the same again from line 172 to line 254, through the eight colours at $20D0, and then a wait for the raster to pass line 255 before the loop starts over. The interrupt is what plays the music, so the loop has nothing else to do.
Twenty-five NOPs nothing reaches, the same padding as at $2031.
Where the bottom bars start in their colour table this frame, 7 down to 0.
The bottom bars' eight colours: blue, grey, yellow, white and back down, ending on blue twice.
Low bytes of 128 pattern addresses, one for each slot of the editor's pattern array: $4000, $4080, $4100 and so on in order to $7F80, so the slots are 128 bytes each and a pattern number is its slot.
High bytes of the same 128 addresses. Nothing in the program writes either table: both come off the disk with the music.

Sixteen tune headers, eight bytes each: the three voices' track addresses (low bytes, then high bytes) and the two tempo counts. Eight of the sixteen have music (0 to 4, 6, 10 and 13), and the four the keys play are 10, 3, 0 and 1. Forty-six of the forty-eight addresses are the slot the track array would give them ($3400 + 192 per tune + 64 per voice); tune 3's third voice and tune 4's second are swapped, so those two tunes play the same third track at $3780.
Low bytes of the frequencies of 96 notes, eight octaves of semitones from 16.4 Hz to 3.9 kHz. The same 192 bytes as Armalyte's table at $C555.
The low-byte table read one note on, for the gap to the next semitone that vibrato works from; from here it runs on to the 96th note.
High bytes of the 96 notes' frequencies.
The high-byte table read one note on, for the vibrato gap; from here it runs on to the 96th note.

The first eight bytes of each of 32 instruments: attack and decay, sustain and release, waveform, effect flags, a spare byte, pulse width high, pulse sweep step, and pulse limits (high nibble the top, low the bottom). Instruments 6 to 10 and 12 to 31 are used; 0 to 4 and 11 are empty, and 5, which is empty too, is played as a rest by two patterns: waveform 0 makes no sound.
The instruments' sustain and release, at +1.
The instruments' waveform, at +2.
The instruments' effect flags, at +3.
The instruments' starting pulse width high byte, at +5.
The instruments' pulse sweep step, at +6 (0 for none).
The pulse sweep limits at +7 of each instrument; from here the table runs on through instruments 1 to 31, eight bytes each in the same order.

The second eight bytes of each instrument: the attack's length in frames, the attack note, the attack waveform, the waveform switched to, the vibrato byte (delay kind in the high nibble, vibrato kind in the low), the arpeggio note (bit 7: relative), and two spare bytes. Not one of the 32 instruments here matches any of Armalyte's 21.
The instruments' attack note (bit 7: relative to the note), at +1.
The instruments' attack waveform, at +2.
The instruments' second waveform for the waveform switch, at +3.
The instruments' vibrato byte, at +4.
The arpeggio note at +5 of each instrument's second entry (bit 7: relative); from here the table runs on through instruments 1 to 31.

Tune 0's three tracks, 64 bytes to a slot, which key 3 plays: patterns 16, 28, 33, 39 and 35 to 37 on the first voice, 17, 27, 30, 32, 34, 36 and 37 on the second, and 15, 29, 31, 37 and 38 on the third. Each ends with $FF and starts again; 21, 25 and 28 entries, the longest tracks here.

Tune 1's three tracks, which key 4 plays: patterns 4 to 6, 19, 21 and 24 on the first voice, 12 to 14, 20, 22 and 25 on the second, 9 to 11, 18, 23 and 26 on the third. Nine or ten entries each, and no pattern played more than twice in a row.
Tune 2's three tracks: one pattern each, 3, 2 and 0, and then $FF to start again. Twelve seconds of music, on no key, with the only use of pattern 0 that a track makes.

Tune 3's first two tracks, which key 2 plays, and in the slot where its third would sit the second voice of tune 4: patterns 40, 43, 44 and 53 to 56 on the first voice, 41, 37 and 46 to 49 over and over on the second. The third track is at $3780.

Tune 4's first voice, which is a slot of zeros: read as a track that is pattern 0 again and again, 256 times over. Its second track is the one at $36C0 and its third is tune 3's, at $3780: the tune is tune 3 with the lead taken out, and no key plays it.
Tune 5's three slots, all zeros: a header pointing at them is a tune of pattern 0 on every voice, which is what the eight empty headers all are.
Tune 6's three tracks, the shortest music here and on no key: pattern 60 on the first voice, 58 nine times then 59 nine times on the second, 57 on the third.
The nine empty slots of tunes 7, 8 and 9.

Tune 10's three tracks, which key 1 plays: the most patterns of any tune here, 61 to 85 across the three voices, in tracks of 29, 30 and 30 entries. Its two long holds are pattern 65 twenty-one times on the first voice against 66 on the second, and pattern 74, one silent note, nine times on each.
The six empty slots of tunes 11 and 12.

Tune 13's first track, and two empty slots. Sixteen entries of zeros come first, so reading it plays pattern 0 four thousand times before the eight real entries (patterns 80, 81, 79, 82, 71, 64, 65 and 74) are reached: a draft left in the array, sharing its patterns with tune 10.
The six empty slots of tunes 14 and 15, the end of the track array.

The pattern array: 128 slots of 128 bytes, a pattern number being its slot. A note is a head byte (the length in beats less one in bits 0-5, bit 6 a rest, bit 7 an extra byte), the extra byte when there is one (an instrument below $80, a slide above it) and the note byte, whose bit 7 ties it to the note after. $FF ends a pattern. Slots 0 to 7: pattern 0 is tune 2's third voice on instruments 17, 18 and 28; 2 and 3 are its other two voices on instrument 24; 4 to 6 are tune 1's first voice on instrument 22, and 5 is the one pattern that uses slides both ways. Slots 1, 7 and 8 hold patterns no track plays: 1 is a single note of the silent instrument 5, and 7 and 8 are eight-note bass lines close to 9 and 10.

Slots 8 to 15: 9, 10 and 11 are tune 1's third voice, sixteen notes each of instruments 17, 18 and 23 alternating a bass note with a drum; 12 to 14 are its second voice on instruments 14, 15, 20 and 23, with the slides that bend the lead; 15 is tune 0's third voice. 8 is unplayed, like 7.

Slots 16 to 23: 16 and 17 open tune 0, four long notes each on instruments 6 and 14; 18, 23 and 19 to 22 belong to tune 1, 18 being its longest pattern at 38 notes; 20 and 22 are its second voice, 19 and 21 its first.

Slots 24 to 31: 24 to 26 end tune 1, and 24 holds the only rest in the whole demo, one beat of silence in fourteen notes. 27 and 30 are tune 0's second voice, 29 and 31 its third, 28 its first; 30 and 31 are thirty-two notes long, the longest patterns here.

Slots 32 to 39: all of them tune 0, and its ending. 33 and 35 are its first voice, 32 34 and 36 its second, 38 its third, 39 its last pattern. 37 is two notes of instrument 23 over six beats, and the only pattern four different tracks play: all three voices of tune 0 and the second of tune 3.

Slots 40 to 47: tune 3. 40, 43 and 44 are its first voice, 41 its second, 42 its third; 46 and 47 are two of the four eight-note runs the second voice cycles through, every note one beat long on instrument 8. Slot 45 is empty.

Slots 48 to 55: 48 and 49 finish tune 3's four runs; 50 to 52 are the drum patterns its third voice shares with tune 4; 53 to 55 are its first voice, with slides in all three. 50 and 51 are sixteen notes of instrument 28.

Slots 56 to 63: 56 ends tune 3's first voice; 57 to 60 are the whole of tune 6, including the pair of four-note runs its second voice plays nine times each; 61 to 63 open tune 10, 63 being thirty-two notes of instruments 9 and 13.

Slots 64 to 71: all tune 10. 64 is four notes of instrument 12 that every voice plays; 65, 66 and 67 are the four-note runs held for twenty-one repeats; 68 to 70 are sixteen-note lines, and 71 is the only pattern that uses instruments 29 and 30.

Slots 72 to 79: tune 10 again. 74 is one note of the silent instrument 5, twelve beats of rest that all three voices use; 73 is thirty-two notes; 75 to 77 and 79 are the lead on instrument 10, which plays nothing else and is used by nothing else.

Slots 80 to 85, the last patterns in the array: tune 10's lead and the ending its first voice plays, all on instrument 10, with 84 shared with the third voice. 81 is twenty-two notes of two beats each. The 42 slots above these, patterns 86 to 127, are empty, as are 45 and 78: 86 of the 128 hold a pattern, and 84 of those are played.
"DEMO LOADER", eleven bytes of PETSCII left in memory by the menu program that loaded this one, four pages above anything this program uses. Nothing here reads it.
